Discard

dis-KARD — stress on second syllable, rhymes with 'card' · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To discard something is to throw it away or get rid of it because it is no longer wanted or needed.

Discard the wilted outer leaves and chop the rest of the cabbage.

Worked Example

The quality control inspector discarded every defective unit without hesitation, knowing they could never reach a customer.

Discard is more precise than 'throw away' because it emphasizes a judgment decision—the items are actively rejected as unsuitable or unwanted, not just removed. The choice about what's no longer worthy of keeping is central to discard.

How Discard Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

Antonyms

keep

keep: to hold on to something valued

cherish

How Strong Is It? — donate → recycle → destroy → discard

donate vs. discard

donate vs. discard: Donate is far gentler than discard — donating passes something you no longer need to someone who can use it, while discarding simply throws it away as unwanted.

recycle vs. discard

recycle vs. discard: Recycle is milder than discard; recycling gets rid of something so it can be made into something new, while discarding tosses it out as worthless.

destroy vs. discard

destroy vs. discard: Destroy is stronger than discard — discarding just throws an unwanted item away, but destroying makes sure it is ruined and can never be used again.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-

Prefix — dis-: away, apart (Latin)

Root — card

Root — card: playing card; stiff sheet of paper (from charta) (Latin (from Greek khartēs))

Put it together

Put it together: Discard literally means 'to throw a card away' — card players in the 1500s discarded the cards they did not want. English kept the image and widened it, so today you can discard anything unwanted, not just a card.

Use the root in a new word: postcard

Use the root in a new word: postcard: A postcard is a stiff little card you mail — the very same card you throw away when you discard something, a word born at the card table.

Word Choice

neutral

Use discard when you want to emphasize that something is being rejected as unwanted or unsuitable—it's stronger than casual 'throw away' and more specific than vague 'get rid of.' For routine disposal or a more casual tone, 'throw away' works fine; reach for discard in contexts where the judgment about what's unwanted matters.
